repos.title: MOST: Memory of Object States and Task Progress for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
repos.paper_summary:
MOST is an end-to-end robot policy that stores long-horizon memory as compressed tokens supervised with subtask progress and object states. RoboCasa-Long is a new benchmark of three multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation tasks. Each sampled timestep yields one token from DINOv2 features of all camera views, and learned future-query tokens are appended. Memory tokens are trained to predict the current subtask and each relevant object's state; these heads are removed at inference. Memory conditions action generation through gated cross-attention in each layer, with no external planner or retrieval.

On RoboCasa365 Target-100%, average success rises from 65.9% (XR-1, a memoryless baseline) to 72.1%. On Target-10%, it rises from 49.6% to 54.6%. On RoboCasa-Long, average maximum task progress rises from 20.83% to 42.22%, and average success rises from 0.00% to 6.66%. Real-world success rises from 6.66% to 43.33%. The visual-history variant MOST-Raw reaches 68.0% on Target-100%, below MOST.

Stated limitations: supervision uses closed-set subtask and object-state vocabularies, full-task success stays low on the longest tasks, and the real-world evaluation uses a fixed-base robot.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Long-horizon manipulation needs object states and task progress kept after they leave view, so MOST stores them in policy memory.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior memory methods mainly vary how much history is kept, while MOST targets which task-state information persists.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: MOST compresses multi-view observations into memory tokens supervised with subtask progress and object states, feeding actions directly.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: MOST raises RoboCasa365 average success from 65.9% to 72.1% and real-world success from 6.66% to 43.33%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: MOST's gains suggest task-state memory helps long repetitive tasks, but success stays limited on the longest tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists model, optimization, input timing, task setup, real-world setup, annotation format, and metric definitions.

repos.title: EarthJev: Calibrated, Non-Generative Answers to Natural-Language Questions about Sentinel-2 Land Cover
repos.paper_summary: EarthJev is a 0.8B-parameter model that answers typed questions about all 12 Sentinel-2 bands without generating text. It widens the input layer of Qwen3.5-0.8B's vision encoder from 3 to 12 channels, copying the RGB kernels and zero-initialising the other nine, and reads each answer from the logits of the option letters at the last position. It is trained with cross-entropy plus Brier score on 70,890 questions from 5% of BigEarthNet v2.0, updating only the widened input layer. On 36,028 test questions it reaches 86.0% accuracy over three seeds, 0.6 and 1.2 points below two 2B multimodal models and 3.5 points below EarthDial-4B, with ECE 0.006. It answers a question in 19.9 ms, 6.8 times faster than the same backbone fine-tuned to generate and 4.3 to 8.7 times faster than the multimodal models, which see only RGB. Replacing the nine non-RGB bands with their mean costs 4.5 points. Limitations: the vision encoder is frozen; a ResNet-50 fixed-vocabulary model is more accurate and faster on the training questions; the questions are template-generated.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Generated answers to satellite-image questions cost decoding time, need parsing, and give no probability.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work either classifies over fixed answer sets or generates free text, and one-pass decision models lack multispectral data.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The answer is read from option-letter logits at one position, and the input layer is widened from three to twelve channels.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and benchmarks
digest_headlines.headline: Questions are generated from reference land-cover masks on a 5% subset of BigEarthNet v2.0, with held-out templates for testing.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: EarthJev is 4.3 to 8.7 times faster per question than multimodal models, with 86.0% accuracy on 36,028 test questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Closed answers, lower accuracy than the 2B and 4B models, and the frozen vision encoder limit what the results support.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Reading option letters at one position is fast and calibrated; the frozen vision encoder is the main limit to address next.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix gives the serialised example state and the question templates, with one unseen template per question type.

repos.title: Decision Models as Policy Gates for Coding Agents: Explicit Policy Boundaries Improve Detection and Reduce False Alarms
repos.paper_summary: The paper tests hosted decision models as classifiers in a multi-rule policy gate for coding-agent tool calls, using a synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls labeled against 28 rules with a sealed holdout. Each model returns a probability per rule, and deterministic policy code makes the allow, block, or ask decision. Across 22 hosted models and two prompted general models, adding examples and counterexamples to rule definitions under a single shared preamble raised recall by 5.5–26.1 points on all 23 available models and reduced false positives on 21. For Jev 1.14, recall rose from 89.3% to 98.2%, and unnecessary interruptions fell from 30.6% to 4.8% of 252 clean actions, with median latency of 120 ms at USD 0.46 per thousand requests. Strong models kept most recall gains when concrete command names were replaced by generic descriptions. On 16 new families, recall improved on 22 of 23 models. Limitations: synthetic data, model-generated labels, a holdout reused after results were seen, a small confirmation set, and runs across different dates.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The paper asks whether hosted decision models can judge a coding agent's proposed tool calls against several policy rules at runtime.

digest_headlines.heading: Prior Literature
digest_headlines.headline: Prior evaluations show model choice depends on the task, and this paper adds per-rule errors with action-level interruption measures.

digest_headlines.heading: Data
digest_headlines.headline: A synthetic set of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules, with a sealed holdout of 1,108 cases.

digest_headlines.heading: Models
digest_headlines.headline: 22 hosted decision models from 15 vendors and two prompted general models were pinned to exact versions.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Two language models wrote examples for fixed rule definitions, scored on a sealed holdout with family-level bootstrap intervals.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Explicit examples raised recall on all 23 models and reduced interruptions for Jev 1.14 from 30.6% to 4.8%.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Explicit boundaries improved detection, while removing concrete names cost strong models little, and eight models met both latency and cost targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Explicit policy boundaries improved detection and usually reduced false alarms; open questions remain on context and thresholds.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results rest on synthetic cases, a reused holdout and runs spread over dates, which bound what the numbers show.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: The dataset includes no real people, organizations, credentials or transcripts, and generative models produced its cases and labels.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the 24 evaluated models with endpoints and identifiers, plus numerical results and rule texts.

repos.title: MemShift: Separating Detection from Repair in LLM-Derived Personal Memory
repos.paper_summary: MemShift is a benchmark that separates two failures of an LLM-derived personal memory: detection, noticing that an input changed, and repair, producing the correct new value. It covers five shifts: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export. The first three fork a synthetic twelve-month world into branches that differ only in the shift. Gold values and dependencies are fixed before text is written, and a deterministic scorer replaces an LLM judge. A memory that logs invalidations gets a per-item diagnosis of missed changes, repair correctness, and served accuracy. The authors also build HoldMem, a reference memory whose detection (keys) and repair (writer re-derivation, exact recomputation, or writer-written programs) can be switched. Across four open-weight models, each writer re-derives at most 25% of changed definition-item values correctly, while exact recomputation gets at least 91% right. Programs over typed records close most of that gap. Limitations: the worlds are synthetic with codified one-sentence definitions, and native systems ran through adapters with no repair check.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Memories that store derived values can fail to notice a change or fail to repair it, and final-answer scores cannot tell which.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Most memory benchmarks score final answers, so a missed detection and a failed repair look the same.

digest_headlines.heading: The MemShift Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: MemShift forks synthetic worlds into branches that differ only in the shift and scores each changed item on detection and repair.

digest_headlines.heading: HoldMem: A Reference Memory
digest_headlines.headline: HoldMem is a reference memory whose detection and repair switches have known effects, used to validate the measure.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments test four open-weight models, two Claude writers, and six existing memory systems on fixed test worlds.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: A detection key helps only when repair is good, and open-weight writers re-derive at most 25% of changed definition values correctly.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Repair decides what detection is worth, and a final-answer score hides which step failed.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: MemShift scores detection and repair separately, and typed-record programs close most of the repair gap on definition items.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Findings rest on synthetic worlds with codified definitions and 20 test worlds, so absolute levels may not transfer.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics Statement
digest_headlines.headline: Benchmark uses only synthetic data, but the work concerns personal profiles that could raise privacy risks.

digest_headlines.heading: Reproducibility Statement
digest_headlines.headline: Worlds, shifts, and probes are generated from seeds with no LLM judge, and the repository regenerates every number in the paper.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers extended related work, stale-value studies, a benchmark audit, mechanics of dependency tracking, and a datasheet.

repos.title: Re$^3$Rank: Listwise Reranking with Reasoning-Conditioned Retrieval Heads
repos.paper_summary: Re3Rank is a listwise reranker that uses a generated reasoning trace, rather than the question alone, as the attention query for scoring candidates. A reasoning generator first writes a trace from the question and up to 50 candidates. A scorer then uses the trace-token positions as the query for a few selected retrieval heads (RRHeads), and each candidate's attention mass from those heads gives a continuous relevance score in one forward pass. The two models are trained jointly with a contrastive cross-entropy plus Recall@k surrogate loss, and a straight-through estimator passes gradients through the discrete trace. RRHeads are selected on an 800-instance seed set. Training uses 38,000 questions from five QA datasets. On nine English benchmarks with Qwen3 backbones at 0.6B, 4B, and 8B, the 4B variant exceeds the strongest of 11 baseline rerankers by 3.11 NDCG@10 points on average, and the 0.6B variant outperforms rerankers up to 32B. Limitations: the trace carries no guarantee of readability, all experiments use one first-stage retriever (Qwen3-Embedding-8B) and top-50 pools, and larger pools are untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: QRHead rerankers may be limited by question-only attention queries, so Re3Rank uses a generated reasoning trace as the query instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: QRHead rerankers score each candidate by the attention mass the question routes to it, with no generated permutation.

digest_headlines.heading: Re3Rank
digest_headlines.headline: Re3Rank trains its generator and scorer jointly, passing the ranking loss through the discrete trace with a straight-through estimator.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the nine-benchmark average, the 4B variant reaches 76.70 Recall@3 and 82.23 NDCG@10, exceeding QRRanker by 3.31 and 3.11 points.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The 0.6B variant surpasses much larger baselines, and the design transfers across backbones, suggesting memory-system use.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Reasoning traces are optimized only for ranking, with no guarantee of readability, and all experiments used one retriever's top-50 pool.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers Qwen3-4B RRHead selection and head-count and redundancy checks, plus full reranking tables.

repos.title: OmniOPD: Stable On-Policy Distillation for Joint Audio-Video Generation
repos.paper_summary:
OmniOPD is a modality-wise on-policy distillation framework that merges separately trained audio and video reinforcement-learning teachers into one joint audio-video student. Each teacher supervises its own modality on trajectories sampled from the student, using a clean-prediction regression loss. Three components address sparse, unstable audio supervision: privileged visual guidance, where the audio teacher sees a less-noisy video input than the student; grouped multi-noise sampling over G trajectories per prompt; and timestep-wise importance weights from a teacher-student transition divergence, with full weight inside a trust region and down-weighting beyond it.

On JavisBench, OmniOPD reaches VQ 3.347 and AQ 5.449, against 2.714 and 5.252 for the LTX-2.3 base. Its DeSync is 0.457, against 0.584 for the base. Its JavisScore is 0.232, below the Audio-Teacher's 0.251. The paper reports preserved audio quality and improved video quality, but its audio-video consistency numbers do not all exceed the teachers. Evaluation relies on JavisBench and VBench, both using automatic metrics.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Joint audio-video training with multiple rewards causes interference, so the authors propose OmniOPD, a modality-wise distillation framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers joint audio-video generators, RL for generative models, and on-policy distillation, and OmniOPD builds on vanilla OPD.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Audio-only reward optimization is unstable and degrades video, and raising audio reward weights does not fix the imbalance.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: The section defines joint audio-video flow matching and the on-policy distillation objective, then shows the OmniOPD overview.

digest_headlines.heading: OmniOPD
digest_headlines.headline: OmniOPD adds asymmetric visual noise for the audio teacher, grouped audio sampling, and a trust-region importance weight.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On JavisBench, OmniOPD gives the highest video quality among distilled models and stronger audio text alignment, with ablations on guidance, coverage, and weighting.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: OmniOPD stabilizes joint audio-video distillation and improves video generation while keeping strong audio performance.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix derives the link between transition divergence and clean-prediction regression, then states limitations and lists qualitative examples.

repos.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting within Self-Learned Neural View-Dependent Color Fields
repos.paper_summary:
This paper adds a learned, view-dependent color field to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) so that Gaussian colors come from a small neural network, aiming for better geometry. Each Gaussian's center queries a hash feature grid, and a 4-layer MLP maps the feature and viewing direction to a color. Training adds self-supervision from the rendered depth: points on the surface are supervised with image colors, and points just before and behind the surface are pushed toward zero color. A Lipschitz bound on the MLP layers limits how fast color can change with position.

On DTU, mean Chamfer distance falls from 1.92 to 1.13 for the 3DGS backbone and from 0.53 to 0.51 for PGSR. The paper reports average gains of 41.1% over 3DGS, 30.0% over FastGS, and 3.8% over 2DGS. On TnT, rendering PSNR for the 3DGS backbone rises from 24.37 to 24.76.

Limitations: the neural color field slightly slows training, and the gain over PGSR is small because PGSR already uses geometry constraints.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Discrete Gaussians often fit geometry poorly, so the method constrains their colors within a smooth neural color field.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior 3DGS geometry methods use constraints or priors, while neural fields' low-frequency bias suggests a geometric regularizer.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Each Gaussian's color comes from a hash grid and network, trained with rendering loss plus surface, free-space and Lipschitz terms.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across object-level and large-scale benchmarks, the method improves geometry for several 3DGS backbones with mixed rendering results.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The method improves 3DGS geometry without external priors, though the appendix notes a small rendering reduction on outdoor scenes.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The funding acknowledgment lists a national science and technology project and a national natural science foundation grant.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers implementation details, extra ablations, depth normalization, outdoor and reflective-region analyses, and limitations.

repos.title: Progressive Multi-Scale Super-Resolution via Cascaded Bicubic Anchors and Inter-Scale Mutual Refinement
repos.paper_summary: PMS-SR is a progressive single-input, multiple-output super-resolution network that produces ×2, ×4, and ×8 outputs in one forward pass, built on a Transformer (CSWin) backbone on the low-resolution grid. Stage 1 predicts each scale as a residual over the detached bicubic upsampling of the previous scale's prediction, with Dirac and zero initialization so training starts exactly at the bicubic cascade. Stage 2, inter-scale mutual refinement, exchanges features in both directions using space-to-depth feedback, deformable cross-scale alignment, and per-pixel softmax fusion, so ×8 features refine the ×2 output. The ×8 refinement runs on the ×4 grid. The model is trained on DF2K with a combined Charbonnier, edge, and frequency loss. On the five standard benchmarks, the 7.95M-parameter model reports the highest PSNR among compared multi-scale methods at ×4 and ×8. At ×8 it beats the ×8-specific DRN-L on all five, and it is within 0.13 dB of the best result elsewhere. Against three single-scale SwinIR-M models, it uses 22% of the parameters and runs 2.9× faster on BSD100 inputs. Limitations: the paper evaluates only on bicubic degradation, and it reports the ×8 refinement cost as one quarter of the ×8-grid cost without a broader efficiency study.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-scale delivery usually needs one model per factor, so the paper trains one network for ×2, ×4 and ×8.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing progressive multi-scale methods pass information only from coarse to fine scales.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each scale is a residual over a detached bicubic cascade, and a second stage then refines all scales jointly.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: PMS-SR has the highest PSNR among compared multi-scale methods in every ×4 and ×8 entry.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The discussion credits three design choices for affordable ×8 and flags weaker ×2 accuracy and no temporal modeling.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A single pass of one 7.95M-parameter model delivers ×2, ×4 and ×8 with 22% of a three-model ladder's parameters.

repos.title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
repos.paper_summary: VeriHarm-Bench is a 150-task benchmark for measuring "harmful success" in LLM coding agents: tasks that an agent completes correctly while also causing an unintended side effect, such as deleting unrelated files. The authors also introduce VeriHarm, an automated framework for building such benchmarks. VeriHarm runs a target agent on a BashBench source task, then has a proposer agent make a minimal benign perturbation (underspecification or delegation of control) and write an executable harm test. The original task-correctness test stays fixed, and failed rollouts guide up to five refinement iterations. LLM judges score candidates on five validity criteria, and the top 150 are kept. The search produced 1,046 candidates in which the agent both completed the task and triggered the harm. On the benchmark, held-out frontier agents averaged 95.1% task accuracy, 58.2% harmful success, and 37.0% safe success. The best agent, GPT-5.6-Sol, completed fewer than 45% of tasks safely. Limitations: the perturbation classes come from prior work, and harm tests must be deterministic and checkable offline.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Coding agents can complete tasks while causing unintended harm, and task-success metrics miss this co-occurrence.

digest_headlines.heading: The VeriHarm Framework
digest_headlines.headline: VeriHarm generates minimal task perturbations with paired executable harm tests, searched over rollouts and scored by judges.

digest_headlines.heading: The VeriHarm-Bench
digest_headlines.headline: The top 150 candidates by consensus judge score form VeriHarm-Bench, checked against a human validity protocol.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Held-out frontier agents average 95.1% task accuracy but only 37.0% safe success on VeriHarm-Bench.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks rely on predefined scenarios or judges; VeriHarm derives perturbations and harm tests automatically from existing tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Task-success metrics can understate coding-agent risk, and the authors offer VeriHarm-Bench as a reproducible testbed.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers limitations, domain coverage, implementation details, target scaffold, taxonomy of elicited harms, full metrics, and construction cost.

repos.title: Sparse Internal Control of Language Models
repos.paper_summary: This paper introduces sparse internal control, which steers a frozen language model by adding inference-time offsets to a small set of internal sites. Two selectors choose the sites: Driver-OMP, which fits the desired displacement by sparse residual fitting, and Coverage-Driver, which greedily maximizes saturated row coverage. Strengths are then refitted jointly under an energy budget and checked against a nonlinear control certificate that bounds target residual, off-target loss, and energy. A six-axis protocol measures reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse. Exploratory experiments cover indirect object identification, MMLU multiple-choice (MCQA), sentiment, and refusal steering. Coverage-Driver and Top-k meet the target criterion on every held-out MCQA and Sentiment P seed and on no F seed. Refusal shows ordered dose response without nominal reachability or reversal. Off-target distribution changes are substantial, and frozen MCQA reuse is weak. Direction rules still require activation contrasts on evaluation pairs, and multi-token generation is untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Frozen language models may be steered by sparse internal interventions, but selecting and evaluating such control interfaces is an open question.

digest_headlines.heading: Sparse internal control
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse internal control is formulated as selecting few site-direction interventions that meet target, preservation, and energy certificates.

digest_headlines.heading: Driver-selection algorithms
digest_headlines.headline: Two selectors, Driver-OMP and Coverage-Driver, choose compact supports from a local linear approximation of the behavioral effects.

digest_headlines.heading: Control evaluation protocol
digest_headlines.headline: A six-axis protocol measures reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback control, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments: sparse internal variables as controllable actuators
digest_headlines.headline: Selected interventions reach targets and reverse behavior under paired-example directions but fail under fixed directions and preserve off-target behavior poorly.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse internal control is presented as a framework and evaluation protocol, with reachability depending on direction information and off-target preservation remaining weak.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix defines the problem, proofs, algorithms, evaluation axes, task settings, constants, extended results, limitations, and reproducibility records.
